storm.summary_layperson: No storms anywhere on radar and the air is far too stable for thunderstorms tonight — just a dry, gusty northwest wind that eases after dark.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound's usual cool-water buffer is already gone (only a 4°F air–water gap at 4 PM), and air falls below the 60°F water temperature by 5 PM — no local storm modifier in play tonight.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: KOKX radar shows no precipitation echoes anywhere in the approach sector, and atmospheric instability (CAPE) is 0 J/kg — there is no fuel for thunderstorms. Upper-level wind shear is fairly strong (32–43 kt from the west, increasing into the evening), but shear alone does nothing without instability. Skies are sunny behind a dry northwest flow.

The only NWS products in effect are fire-weather statements, not storm alerts. NWS Upton has Special Weather Statements for an elevated risk of fire spread across southern Connecticut into early evening: dry fuels, northwest gusts of 25–35 mph, and humidity near 40%. Use care with any outdoor ignition sources; the statements expire by 7 PM.

Local effects: On storm days the cove is often protected by a stable layer of cool air over Long Island Sound — the Sound holds its temperature while the land and air around it swing, so when the air is warmer than the water, incoming storms tend to weaken at the shoreline. Today that buffer is essentially absent: the air–water gap is only 4°F at 4 PM (below the ~5°F threshold where it matters), and with sunset at 5:52 PM the air drops to about 60°F by 5 PM and ~53°F by 7 PM — colder than the 60°F Sound. There is no sea breeze either; the wind is a straight offshore northwest flow.

Most likely outcome: dry, clear evening in the cove and in surrounding towns alike — no difference between the shoreline and inland because there is nothing for the Sound to modify.

What would change the call: nothing in the current data points that way. A new radar echo upstream to the west, or any instability showing up in the next model run, would be the trigger to re-check — neither is expected tonight.

wind.regime_label: Fresh northwest gradient wind — no sea breeze in play
wind.tactics_blurb: Big, puffy offshore northwest breeze at the start of the window — stay in the middle of the cove away from the lee of the western shore and play the 15–30° shifts puff by puff. It eases steadily after the 5:52 PM sunset but doesn't die.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Regime: moderate-to-fresh gradient wind — no sea breeze in play. The air–water temperature difference is only 4°F (a sea breeze needs at least 5°F), and not a single coastal station shows a southerly component. Well-sited anemometers around the region average 14.2 kt from the northwest, right at the top of the moderate band, and the NWS forecast agrees: NW ~15 kt with gusts to ~24 kt. This is synoptic wind behind a departing system, so it does not depend on the sun.

Now at RYC (4 PM): NW 313° at 19.7 kt, 10-minute average 17.7 kt, gusting 30 kt. The western Sound buoy shows 21 kt gusting 28 kt. That's big breeze — lighter dinghies will be overpowered at the start of the window and gusts near 30 kt are postponement territory for small boats.

Why the middle of the cove: northwest is an offshore wind here — it crosses land, trees and houses before reaching the water, so it arrives as distinct puffs with big direction swings (15–30°) and holes in between. Pressure is best on average mid-cove, away from the immediate lee of the western shore. Look upwind for dark patches and sail to them; tack on the headers rather than committing to one side.

Through the window: sunset is 5:52 PM. Since this is gradient wind, it won't collapse the way a sea breeze does, but as the land cools after dark the lowest layer of air stabilizes and stops mixing the stronger winds aloft down to the surface. Expect roughly 16 kt at 5 PM easing to ~13 kt by 6 PM and ~10 kt by 8 PM, with the gust spread shrinking and the course getting noticeably steadier after 7 PM. Direction holds NW, perhaps veering a little toward NNW late.

Model vs. observations: the HRRR model has 10-meter wind at only ~11 kt WNW (296°) for 4 PM, while stations are already at NW–NNW (313–328°) and RYC is reading nearly 18 kt sustained — a 32° direction gap and a ~6 kt speed gap. Speeds above are anchored to RYC and follow the model's downward trend; directions follow RYC rather than the model. HRRR hours past 7 PM did not download, so the 8–10 PM rows are an extrapolation of that trend and carry lower confidence.

Fleet impact: early window — 15–20 kt with 25+ kt gusts, survival conditions for lighter dinghies, keelboats fine with reefs. From about 7 PM the cove settles into the 8–11 kt sweet spot for one-designs, though by then it's dark.

data_caveats: HRRR forecast hours past 7 PM unavailable — 8–10 PM wind rows extrapolated from the evening trend (lower confidence)
HRRR running ~6 kt light and ~30° backed versus observed winds; wind numbers anchored to Riverside YC observations
NWS forecast period covers this afternoon only, not the evening
Buoy 44040 (western Sound) stale — last reading 75 min ago
White Plains (KHPN), Islip, Westhampton, Farmingdale and Willimantic airport wind sensors offline
Two Port Chester / Rye APRS stations stale (4–5 hr old)
